results.gap_diagnosis: Step 1 (Level): The target Constructive mode is not achieved. The teacher is merely checking administrative status ('have you guys um started cutting the foam board') which keeps students in a passive or basic active compliance state. Step 2 (Breadth): Active speaker coverage is 0.0% (0 out of 30 students). No student is speaking or generating externalized cognitive artifacts; they are silent recipients of a deadline warning.
results.proposed_rewrite: Transition the administrative status check into an individual planning task. Instead of asking if they have started, instruct each student to independently draft a personalized fabrication sequence and self-assess their structural risks based on their own design drawings.
results.scaffolding_strategy: First, implement an Individual Milestone Mapping task where each student spends 3 minutes drawing a personalized timeline for the remaining 6 days. Second, introduce a Self-Diagnostic Prompt, requiring students to write down the most fragile joint in their drawing and formulate an individual strategy to cut it without tearing the foam.
results.new_question: Please take out your submitted project drawing. On a blank sheet of paper, write down the exact sequence of cuts you will make to assemble your physical model, and detail how you will modify your blade pressure to handle the most delicate piece of your specific design.
results.reference_answer: First, I will cut the base plate to establish the foundation. The most delicate piece is the curved archway; to avoid tearing the foam, I will make three light, progressive scoring cuts using a fresh blade held at a 45-degree angle, rather than trying to cut all the way through on the first pass.

results.gap_diagnosis: Step 1 (Level): The highest cognitive level achieved by students is merely active (raising hands to acknowledge trouble: 'i see one i see two three'), which fails to reach the target Constructive (C) mode. Students are passively receiving the teacher's explanations of cutting variables rather than generating their own cognitive insights. Step 2 (Breadth): Out of 30 students, active speaker coverage is 0.0%. A tiny fraction (three students) briefly signaled trouble physically, while the vast majority remain entirely silent and disengaged from active knowledge construction.
results.proposed_rewrite: Shift the instruction from a passive lecture on cutting tips to an individual diagnostic task. Instead of telling students why cuts go wrong, the teacher must prompt each student to independently analyze their own physical cutting artifacts, identify specific defects, and construct a personalized troubleshooting protocol based on blade angle, sharpness, and pressure.
results.scaffolding_strategy: Implement an 'Individual Cut-Edge Audit'. Direct each student to examine their most recent foam board cut under a light. Have them independently complete a 'Mechanical Defect Map' where they sketch the cross-section of their cut (noting if the paper is torn, the foam is melted/crushed, or the line is jagged) and write a self-diagnosis attributing the defect to a specific physical variable (e.g., blade angle vs. excessive downforce) along with their planned corrective action.
results.new_question: Examine the edge of your most recent foam board cut. Based on the physical texture of the cut—whether the paper backing is torn, the foam core is crushed, or the line is jagged—individually write down a diagnosis explaining exactly which cutting variable (blade age, handle angle, or downward pressure) caused that specific defect and how you will physically adjust your technique on the next slice.
results.reference_answer: My cut has a jagged, shredded foam core and the bottom paper layer is torn rather than sliced. This indicates a dull blade combined with too much downward pressure in a single pass. Because the blade isn't sharp enough to shear the paper, my heavy downward force ended up crushing and dragging the foam. To correct this, I will snap to a fresh blade segment, lower the knife angle closer to 30 degrees, and execute three light, swift passes instead of trying to force it in one go.

results.gap_diagnosis: Step 1 (Level): The highest cognitive level achieved is Active (listening and following along with the screen share), which fails to reach the Constructive target. The transcript shows a teacher monologue explaining composition errors ('there's been a few of you that have... just put... decorations in the corners') without asking students to generate any designs or construct explanations. Step 2 (Breadth): Active speakers represent 0% of the class (0 out of 30). The entire class remains passive or silently active, with zero student verbal output or individual cognitive generation recorded in this segment.
results.proposed_rewrite: Transition the lesson from a passive demonstration of composition rules to an individual construction task. Instead of telling students what 'continuance' looks like, the teacher should direct each student to analyze their own current drawing, identify one area of static symmetry, and sketch a physical modification that forces continuance past the border.
results.scaffolding_strategy: Implement an 'Individual Composition Audit'. First, have every student place their physical drawing on their desk and use a sticky note to mask out one quadrant. Instruct them to write down on the sticky note a self-critique of how that quadrant behaves (e.g., 'static', 'symmetrical', or 'floating'). Second, have each student sketch a revised thumbnail of that quadrant on the sticky note, deliberately extending at least one structural line past the boundary to construct a 'window frame' effect.
results.new_question: Look closely at your own sketch. Identify one shape that is currently 'floating' inside the border. Redraw that shape on a separate piece of paper so that it intersects the edge, and write a brief explanation describing how this specific change transforms your border from a static picture frame into a dynamic window frame.
results.reference_answer: In my original drawing, the geometric star was floating entirely in the upper right corner, making it look like a static sticker. I have redrawn it so that the top two points of the star are cropped out by the top border. This creates continuance because the viewer's eye now has to imagine the rest of the star extending beyond the page, converting the border into a window frame.

No student has generated or constructed any individual output. Step 2 (Breadth): The active speaker count is 0 (0.0% coverage) out of 30 students. The entire class is silent, meaning there is a complete lack of active participation or cognitive processing regarding this scheduling update.
results.proposed_rewrite: Transition this passive administrative announcement into an individual time-management and goal-setting task. Instead of just receiving the new hours, each student will individually analyze their own weekly schedule and construct a personal office hour attendance plan tailored to their current academic needs.
results.scaffolding_strategy: Implement an 'Individual Schedule Mapping' task. Provide students with a template listing the new time blocks (10-12 AM and 6-8 PM on Mon, Tue, Wed, Fri). Instruct each student to independently compare these blocks with their own class schedule, identify their personal free windows, and write down one specific topic or question they currently need help with that they could bring to that session.

results.reference_answer: According to my schedule, the Tuesday evening block from 6:00 to 7:00 PM is my only free window. I have written down that I will use this time to ask for feedback on my draft for the upcoming research proposal.

results.gap_diagnosis: Step 1 (Level): The highest cognitive level reached is indeed Constructive (C). A single student actively constructs an inquiry regarding the project submission format, asking, 'how do you want us to turn in the project' and 'is there any format like how do we take the pictures or'. Step 2 (Breadth): While the target level is achieved, coverage is severely bottlenecked at 3.3% (1 out of 30 students). The rest of the class remains passive listeners to the teacher's monologue about office hours and the single student's query, failing to construct their own understanding of the submission process.
results.proposed_rewrite: To scale this constructive cognitive behavior from one student to the entire class of 30, the teacher must transition from an interactive monologue to an individual construction task. Instead of simply answering the single student, the teacher should prompt every student to individually construct a personal submission checklist and identify one specific project hurdle they need resolved during office hours.
results.scaffolding_strategy: Implement an 'Individual Submission Checklist & Office Hour Prompting' strategy. First, ask each student to independently draft a three-step technical workflow for formatting and uploading their specific project files. Second, have each student self-assess their current project draft and write down one precise, personalized question they would ask during office hours to resolve their biggest bottleneck.
results.new_question: Before I share my screen, I want every student to take two minutes to write down your own individual three-step plan for how you will format and upload your project photos, along with one specific technical question you need answered during office hours to complete it.
results.reference_answer: My three-step plan: 1. Take high-resolution JPEG photos of my physical sketches under natural light. 2. Convert the JPEGs into a single, organized PDF document. 3. Upload the PDF to the Canvas portal by Sunday. My office hours question is: 'If my file size exceeds the Canvas limit, should I compress the PDF or upload a link to a cloud drive?'

results.gap_diagnosis: Step 1 (Level): The highest cognitive level achieved is currently Passive (P), as students are only listening to the teacher's instructions ('okay so when you're ready to turn in...'). No constructive behavior is present. Step 2 (Breadth): Active speaker coverage is 0.0% (0 out of 30 students). The entire class is silent, meaning the target Constructive mode is completely unachieved across all students, with zero independent output generated.
results.proposed_rewrite: Shift the passive explanation of submission guidelines into an individual visual planning task. Instead of telling students how to take the photos, the teacher will require each student to independently formulate a customized photography plan and visual checklist tailored to the unique geometry of their own project.
results.scaffolding_strategy: First, implement an Individual Camera Mapping exercise where each student independently drafts a schematic diagram indicating the four camera placements around their specific 3D model. Second, guide students through a Solo Self-Diagnostic Checklist creation, where they write down three personalized criteria that their photos must meet to clearly demonstrate the volume of their specific project.
results.new_question: On your own sketchpad, draw a top-down diagram of your sculpture. Individually mark the four camera positions and heights you will use to capture its volume, and write a brief note explaining why these exact angles prevent your 3D depth from looking flat.
results.reference_answer: I sketched a top-down view of my asymmetrical clay piece. I marked Camera Position 1 at 45 degrees elevation from the front-left to capture the main curve, Position 2 at 135 degrees to show the hollow interior, Position 3 at 225 degrees for the back support, and Position 4 at 315 degrees to show the overall width. This plan ensures that my photos show the actual volume rather than looking like flat, two-dimensional shapes.

Only 1 out of 30 students (3.3% coverage) is actively constructing their understanding, while the remaining 29 students are listening passively to the teacher's monologue about cheating and project guidelines without producing any individual output.
results.proposed_rewrite: To scale the constructive behavior from the single active speaker to the entire class, the teacher should transition from a lecture-style explanation to an individual mapping activity. Instead of just answering the question verbally, the teacher will prompt every student to individually construct their own project timeline and checklist based on the criteria mentioned.

Second, students must individually write down their own 'Quality Control Checklist' specifying how they will ensure their photos are clear and what their 10-second video will demonstrate, forcing each student to cognitively organize the project requirements on their own.

My 10-second video will show the origami structure unfolding from a closed flat state to its fully open 3D state, shot near my window for bright, clear natural lighting.

results.gap_diagnosis: Step 1 (Level): The target constructive mode ('c') is technically achieved by a single student who is actively clarifying and planning their material sourcing ('you said you could get all the materials in home depot'). Step 2 (Breadth): However, breadth is extremely limited with only 1 active speaker out of 30 (3.3% coverage). The rest of the class is passively listening to the teacher's lecture on wire specifications ('what you don't want to do is get the kind that's... square shape') without individually processing how these physical properties will impact their upcoming hands-on exercises.
results.proposed_rewrite: To scale the constructive mode to all 30 silent students, the teacher will shift from a passive lecture on procurement to an individual cognitive modeling task. Every student will independently analyze the physical properties of the recommended round wire versus the contraindicated square wire, mapping out how these material differences will directly affect their individual drafting and bending techniques.
results.scaffolding_strategy:
1. Individual Tension Analysis: Have each student open their digital journal and independently sketch a cross-sectional diagram comparing how force is distributed when bending a round wire versus a square-edged wire.
2. Solo Execution Checklist: Instruct each student to write down their own step-by-step sequence for preparing and straightening the wire before Monday's exercise, forcing them to individually synthesize the SKU requirements and tool constraints.
results.new_question: Before you purchase your materials, I want each of you to individually sketch a diagram in your design journal illustrating how force distributes differently when bending a round wire versus a square wire, and write down one specific reason why the round wire's geometry prevents the formation of permanent kinks.
results.reference_answer: When bending a round wire, the circular cross-section distributes the bending tension uniformly across the entire surface, allowing for smooth, gradual curves. A square wire, however, concentrates stress along its rigid flat faces and 90-degree corners, which forces the metal to fold sharply and create permanent kinks that are extremely difficult to straighten out.

results.gap_diagnosis: Step 1 (Level): Currently, student cognitive level is Passive (P). The teacher is delivering a monologue about wire selection and tools ('with galvanized wire it doesn't work right... has to be this wire'). No student speaks (0.0% coverage) or constructs any explanations, meaning the target Constructive (C) mode is not achieved. Step 2 (Breadth): The active speaker count is 0 out of 30, showing that the entire class is silent and merely receiving information rather than actively processing or constructing concepts individually.
results.proposed_rewrite: Instead of lecturing on why galvanized wire fails, the teacher should prompt students to individually analyze the visual and mechanical properties of different wires. Students will independently construct a rationalization for material selection based on the project's goal of emulating a pencil line.
results.scaffolding_strategy: Have each student individually write a brief visual-impact comparison between matte black wire and galvanized wire. Then, prompt each student to independently inspect their own household tools and write down a single-sentence justification of how their specific pliers will help them manipulate the wire.
results.new_question: Please write down an individual analysis explaining how the physical properties of matte black wire versus reflective galvanized wire affect the visual contrast and line quality of your final photograph.
results.reference_answer: Matte black wire absorbs light, which creates a sharp, high-contrast silhouette against a white background, perfectly mimicking a dark graphite pencil mark. In contrast, galvanized wire reflects light, causing glare and highlights that break the illusion of a continuous, flat 2D line.

results.gap_diagnosis: Step 1 (Level): The target interactive mode (i) is achieved conceptually, as seen when students actively co-examine design techniques with the instructor, such as discussing circle-cutting workarounds ('sand the edge nice and smooth') and brainstorming narrative titles. Step 2 (Breadth): This interaction is highly bottlenecked. Only 6 out of 30 students (20% coverage) are participating in this dialogue. The remaining 80% are passive listeners. To achieve true interactive scaling, the constructive process of building design narratives and troubleshooting physical constraints must be shifted from a teacher-student monologue to student-student collaborative design-tuning.
results.proposed_rewrite: Transform the individual narrative and technical troubleshooting session into a structured peer-to-peer 'Narrative Exchange and Technical Hack' workshop. Instead of the teacher suggesting titles and cutting techniques individually, students will work in pairs to analyze each other's visual forms, co-create design narratives, and collaboratively pitch structural improvements.
results.scaffolding_strategy: Implement the 'Blind Narrative Swap'. Partners exchange high-resolution photos of their current 3D maquettes without providing any context. Partner A must interpret the visual hierarchy of Partner B's piece and propose three conceptual titles using the teacher's 'found-word' constraints (e.g., jazz track titles or color-chip names), explaining how the physical layers support that title. Partner B then critiques these proposals, and together they negotiate a final narrative title. They must also co-write one actionable technical solution for any cutting or leveling issues identified in their models.
results.new_question: With your partner, examine their design without hearing their explanation. Based purely on their visual composition, what jazz track title or color-sample name best captures the rhythm of their layers? Discuss together: how can you adjust the physical layout to make this shared narrative even more apparent?
results.reference_answer: My partner, Marcus, showed me his piece with the sharp, repeating diagonal cuts. I proposed the jazz title 'Take Five' because the alternating angles look like a syncopated 5/4 rhythm. Marcus liked that but noted the flat base made it feel too heavy. Together, we decided that if he adds two thin, elevated foam slivers underneath the main structure, it will create a deep shadow line, making the 'rhythm' look like it is floating off the board.

Step 2 (Breadth): However, the active speaker count is only 2 out of 30 (6.7% coverage). The constructive cognitive processing is confined to a private consultation. Instead of just approving April's approach, the instructor will prompt every student to independently audit their own project proposals for academic integrity and self-plagiarism boundaries.

I will individually transform it by applying a digital vector rendering style and a completely different color palette, ensuring that the final output is a new conceptual exploration of space rather than a replication of my old work.
